classification.difficultyReason: Translate a variable quantity and three additional pencils into one additive expression.

questions.mappingNote: The assigned task applies the same additive situation with x already supplied, directly assessing translation from words to an algebraic expression.
questions.methodNote: Example 1 represents the unknown number of pencils in a case by x and adds the three other pencils. The expression-meaning table identifies addition with a sum or an increased quantity.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate a variable quantity and three additional pencils into one additive expression.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate familiar addition and subtraction phrases, preserving operand order for 'subtracting from' and 'less than'; each part needs only one operation.

questions.mappingNote: Each part directly assesses translation from verbal addition or subtraction descriptions into algebraic expressions, matching translate-expressions.
questions.methodNote: Example 2 translates sums, 'subtracting from', 'less than' and differences into expressions, and reorders a three-term sum. The page 4 table reinforces addition and subtraction vocabulary.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct translation of addition and subtraction descriptions using the taught vocabulary.

classification.difficultyReason: Directly translate product, multiplication and quotient descriptions into single-operation expressions.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts assess translating words into algebraic expressions. Retain explicit operation signs at this introductory stage; part c uses the teacher's equivalent factor order.
questions.methodNote: Example 3 on PDF page 3 translates product and quotient descriptions using explicit multiplication and division signs. The expression-meaning table on PDF page 4 reinforces these forms.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Directly translate product, multiplication and quotient descriptions into single-operation expressions.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate familiar product and difference language, then two successive operations, directly into expressions.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and b apply the product convention from Example 3; c applies the difference convention from Example 2; d–f apply the multiplication-then-addition-or-subtraction structure from Example 4 and the expression table.
questions.methodNote: Example 2 translates difference language into subtraction. Examples 3 and 4 retain explicit multiplication signs and translate successive operations in order. The page 4 expression table reinforces these meanings.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate familiar product and difference language, then two successive operations, directly into expressions.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate explicit operation descriptions, including division followed by addition or subtraction.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and b use the two-operation translation demonstrated in the page 4 table; part c uses the sums taught in Example 2; part d extends the product wording in Example 3 to three factors.
questions.methodNote: Translate words directly into operations, retaining explicit multiplication and division signs as taught in Examples 2–4 and the expression-meaning table. Apply division before the subsequent addition or subtraction.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate explicit operation descriptions, including division followed by addition or subtraction.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate a single removal of 20 objects into subtraction from a pronumeral.

questions.mappingNote: Question 6 applies the same removal model as Example 5, with n apricots initially and 20 removed; translating the situation is the directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Example 5 represents an original quantity by a pronumeral and subtracts the number removed. The expression table also identifies subtraction from a pronumeral.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate a single removal of 20 objects into subtraction from a pronumeral.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate equal groups directly into a product, following Example 6.

questions.mappingNote: Question 7 applies the same equal-group model to five boxes of x chocolates; translating the situation into a product is the directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Example 6 on PDF page 3 represents three equal boxes of x marbles as 3 × x. The expression table on PDF page 4 likewise retains explicit multiplication signs.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate equal groups directly into a product, following Example 6.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate a single equal-sharing situation into a division expression.

questions.mappingNote: Question 8 uses the same equal-sharing method, with bananas shared among 3 people. Retain division-sign notation at this stage.
questions.methodNote: Example 7 on PDF page 4 represents equal sharing of n oranges among 5 people as n ÷ 5. Earlier examples establish pronumerals and arithmetic expressions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate a single equal-sharing situation into a division expression.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate a deposit into addition to an unknown starting balance.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed task translates a bank deposit into an algebraic expression; no numerical substitution or simplification is required.
questions.methodNote: Represent the unknown amount with its given pronumeral and express an increase using addition, as in Example 1 and the expression-meaning table.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate a deposit into addition to an unknown starting balance.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate a single age comparison into an addition expression.

questions.mappingNote: The task directly assesses translating '5 years older' into adding 5 to x.
questions.methodNote: Represent the known age by its pronumeral and translate an additional amount using addition, following Example 1 and the addition expressions on page 4.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate a single age comparison into an addition expression.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise that a square's perimeter comprises four equal sides and express one side by dividing x by four.

questions.mappingNote: Divide the given perimeter by the square's four equal sides; the directly assessed skill is translating the context into an expression.
questions.methodNote: Example 7 on PDF page 4 expresses equal sharing using division, retaining the division sign. Earlier examples translate contextual quantities into algebraic expressions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate equal sharing of a square's perimeter among its four equal sides into a division expression.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate equal groups of eight into a single multiplication expression.

questions.mappingNote: Question 12 applies the equal-groups method to m boxes with eight toffees in each box, requiring translation into an algebraic expression.
questions.methodNote: Example 6 represents equal groups by explicit multiplication; Example 3 and the expression-meaning table retain the multiplication sign.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate equal groups of eight into a single multiplication expression.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret the unknown number as the missing addend and subtract n from the stated total of 10.

questions.mappingNote: Finding the other addend from a total of 10 requires translating the stated relationship into 10 minus n.
questions.methodNote: Translate the situation directly into an expression using subtraction, following Example 2 and Example 5 and the expression-meaning table.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Express the missing addend using one subtraction.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate a single increase into an algebraic expression.

questions.mappingNote: The original n cards correspond to the unknown starting quantity; collecting 20 more requires adding 20.
questions.methodNote: Represent an unknown quantity by a pronumeral and express an increase using addition, as in Example 1 and the addition meanings table.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate a single increase into an algebraic expression.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate the explicitly stated three equal sides into equal sharing of the total length s.

questions.mappingNote: The three equal sides share the total length s equally; translating this relationship directly assesses forming an algebraic expression.
questions.methodNote: Example 7 represents equal sharing by dividing the total pronumeral by the number of equal shares, using explicit division notation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate an equal-sharing situation into division of a pronumeral by 3.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct application of the multiplication and power notation demonstrated in Example 8.

questions.mappingNote: All twelve parts directly assess these notation conventions; part l retains addition between its two terms.
questions.methodNote: Example 8 demonstrates omitting multiplication signs, placing numerical coefficients first, multiplying numerical factors and expressing repeated variable factors as powers. Page 7 summarises these conventions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct application of the multiplication and power notation demonstrated in Example 8.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct application of multiplication and power notation, with numerical factors combined.

questions.mappingNote: Every part directly assesses the notation conventions demonstrated on page 6.
questions.methodNote: Omit multiplication signs, put the numerical coefficient first, and express repeated identical factors using powers; Example 8 combines numerical factors.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct application of multiplication and power notation, with numerical factors combined.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct conversion of division notation to fraction notation.

questions.mappingNote: All eight parts reproduce Example 9's numerical or pronumeral division forms.
questions.methodNote: Write the dividend above the fraction bar and the divisor below it, as in Example 9.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct conversion of division notation to fraction notation.

classification.difficultyReason: Reverse multiplication and power notation into explicit factors.

questions.mappingNote: The task explicitly asks for multiplication signs rather than evaluation or expansion of brackets.
questions.methodNote: Reverse the stated product and power conventions; a square represents two identical factors.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Reverse multiplication and power notation into explicit factors.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct reversal of fraction notation into division notation.

questions.mappingNote: This reverses Example 9; part d retains the numerator product mn as one dividend.
questions.methodNote: Read a fraction as its complete numerator divided by its denominator.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct reversal of fraction notation into division notation.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate product, quotient and two-operation descriptions using the newly introduced notation.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–f use Examples 3, 8–10 and the notation summary; g–h use Example 4's multiplication followed by addition or subtraction.
questions.methodNote: Translate product and quotient language, then apply coefficient-first, fraction and power notation. Preserve the order of operations in two-step descriptions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate product, quotient and two-operation descriptions using the newly introduced notation.

classification.difficultyReason: Represent equal sharing with one algebraic quotient.

questions.mappingNote: Example 7 supplies the equal-sharing model; Example 9 supplies the required algebraic division notation.

classification.difficultyReason: Represent five equal quantities using one algebraic product.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Represent five equal quantities using one algebraic product.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate two passenger capacities into products and add them.

questions.mappingNote: Represent each type of minibus by capacity times number of vehicles, then add the two capacities.
questions.methodNote: Example 6 represents equal groups by multiplication. Pages 6–7 omit multiplication signs and write numerical coefficients first.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate two passenger capacities into products and add them.

classification.difficultyReason: Form two cost products and add them using algebraic notation.

questions.mappingNote: Each cost is price per kilogram multiplied by kilograms; adding the costs assesses translation into an expression.
questions.methodNote: Examples 4–6 translate contextual operations into expressions. Pages 6–7 write products with numerical coefficients first and omit multiplication signs.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Form two cost products and add them using algebraic notation.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate direct descriptions of squares, cubes and addition into notation.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts translate verbal descriptions; powers are the notation needed to express the repeated factors.
questions.methodNote: Page 6 introduces repeated factors as powers. Page 7 names squares and cubes, and Example 10 translates verbal descriptions into power notation. Example 4 on page 3 combines multiplication with addition.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate direct descriptions of squares, cubes and addition into notation.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute one positive integer into simple addition expressions.

questions.mappingNote: Every part replaces a with 3 and evaluates an addition expression, directly assessing substitution into expressions.
questions.methodNote: Page 9 defines substitution as replacing a pronumeral with a particular value. Example 11a substitutes into an addition expression and then evaluates; Examples 12 and 13 on page 10 reinforce substitution before arithmetic.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute one positive integer into simple addition expressions.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute one positive integer into four single-subtraction expressions.

questions.mappingNote: Each part replaces m with 9 and evaluates one subtraction, directly assessing substitution into expressions.
questions.methodNote: Page 9 defines substitution as replacing a pronumeral with a particular value. Example 11 demonstrates replacement followed by evaluation; page 10 Example 12(a) demonstrates subtraction after substitution.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute one positive integer into four single-subtraction expressions.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute one positive integer into a single algebraic product.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts directly assess replacing x with 4 and evaluating a coefficient multiplied by that value, following Example 11b.
questions.methodNote: Page 9 defines substitution and Example 11b replaces x with 4 in 5x, explicitly writes multiplication and evaluates. Page 10 continues substitution in Examples 12 and 13.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute one positive integer into a single algebraic product.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute one positive integer into four simple quotients and evaluate.

questions.mappingNote: Each part directly applies Example 11c with x=24 and the printed denominator retained.
questions.methodNote: Page 9 defines substitution as replacing a pronumeral with its given value. Example 11c substitutes 4 into x/2, writes 4/2 and evaluates to 2. Page 10 continues numerical substitution in Examples 12 and 13.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute one positive integer into four simple quotients and evaluate.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute each positive integer into a single squared pronumeral and evaluate.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts directly assess substitution into x squared, following Example 11d.
questions.methodNote: The substitution introduction and Example 11d replace the pronumeral with its given value, then evaluate the square. Examples 12 and 13 reinforce substitution and evaluating powers before other operations.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute each positive integer into a single squared pronumeral and evaluate.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute one positive integer and evaluate two-operation expressions.

questions.methodNote: Example 12 substitutes both given pronumerals and calculates products before subtraction.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute a positive integer and evaluate its square before multiplication and addition or subtraction.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute the number of rows into the given expression for the number of seats.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute the number of rows into the given expression for the number of seats.

classification.difficultyReason: Compare variable factors and powers while ignoring coefficients, recognising that reversing factor order preserves a product.

questions.mappingNote: Every part asks only for identification of like or unlike terms. Parts c and h use reversed factor order; parts f and g distinguish powers, directly matching Example 14.
questions.methodNote: Compare pronumerals and their indices. Different coefficients do not prevent terms being like; multiplication order does not change the variable product. Page 12 Example 14 demonstrates each distinction.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct recognition of matching pronumerals and powers, including reversed factor order.

classification.difficultyReason: Group separated x and y terms and combine their coefficients while carrying subtraction signs with the correct terms.

questions.mappingNote: Every part directly assesses collecting like terms; parts g–i additionally require regrouping separated like terms, as demonstrated by the preceding teaching.
questions.methodNote: Identify terms with the same pronumerals and indices, regroup where necessary, and add or subtract their coefficients. Example 15 demonstrates single-pronumeral and two-pronumeral expressions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct addition and subtraction of like terms, including regrouping terms in two pronumerals, following Example 15.

classification.difficultyReason: Form each sum, check whether variable factors and powers match, and combine coefficients only for like terms.

questions.mappingNote: All eight parts require forming a sum; six collect like terms and two retain unlike terms. Collecting like terms is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Identify matching pronumerals and indices, then add coefficients using the distributive law. Leave unlike terms as a sum, following the explanations on page 12 and Examples 15–16.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Forms sums of two terms and combines coefficients when their pronumeral parts match, including squared and multivariable terms.

classification.difficultyReason: Distinguish squared from linear terms, regroup separated matching terms, and subtract coefficients without losing their signs.

questions.mappingNote: Example 16 demonstrates collecting single-variable, product and squared terms, including expressions containing both squared and linear terms; these directly match parts a–j.
questions.methodNote: Identify terms with identical pronumerals and indices. Reorder terms where necessary, then add or subtract their coefficients, retaining unlike terms separately.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Collect coefficients of like terms, distinguishing linear and squared terms as demonstrated in Example 16.

classification.difficultyReason: Add two algebraic terms, recognising equivalent variable order and retaining unlike terms.

questions.mappingNote: Question 5 directly applies the like-term definition and distributive explanation on page 12, Example 14's ab=ba reasoning, and Examples 15–16's collection of coefficients on pages 12–13.
questions.methodNote: Identify terms with the same pronumerals and indices, use commutativity to recognise reordered products, then add coefficients using the distributive law. Unlike terms remain separate.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Add two algebraic terms, recognising equivalent variable order and retaining unlike terms.

classification.difficultyReason: Collect matching terms, including recognising reversed variable products as equivalent and interpreting an unwritten coefficient as one.

questions.mappingNote: Every part directly assesses collecting like terms. Parts g and h additionally require recognising equivalent variable orders, as taught in Example 14.
questions.methodNote: The like-terms explanation uses the distributive law to combine coefficients. Examples 15 and 16 add or subtract like terms while retaining unlike terms; Example 14 explains that variable order does not affect a product.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Collect coefficients of like terms, recognising that reversing variable order leaves a product unchanged.

classification.difficultyReason: Represent five consecutive whole numbers algebraically and use collected terms to justify a general divisibility claim.

questions.mappingNote: Collecting the five copies of the pronumeral and the constant terms is the central assessed algebraic skill; the final factor of 5 establishes the required general claim.
questions.methodNote: Represent consecutive numbers using a pronumeral, collect like terms as demonstrated in Examples 15–16, and express the resulting sum as five times a whole number.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Represent five consecutive whole numbers algebraically and use collected terms to justify a general divisibility claim.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate explicitly ordered addition or subtraction followed by multiplication into bracketed expressions.

questions.mappingNote: Every part translates a verbal sequence into an expression; the brackets preserve the specified first operation. The supplied reuse candidates assess different tasks and are not source-equivalent.
questions.methodNote: Examples 17 and 18 bracket the first addition or subtraction, then write the multiplying number before the brackets without a multiplication sign.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate explicitly ordered addition or subtraction followed by multiplication into bracketed expressions.

classification.difficultyReason: Track the stated order of two operations and use brackets when multiplication acts on the entire preceding sum or difference.

questions.mappingNote: Each part translates verbal operations into an expression; parts b and d require brackets around the first result.
questions.methodNote: Examples 17 and 18 form the first operation inside brackets, then move the multiplying factor to the front. Example 19 contrasts multiplication of a bracketed sum with multiplication followed by addition.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate two successive operations, distinguishing whether brackets are required.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct substitution of one positive integer, followed by bracket evaluation and ordinary arithmetic.

questions.mappingNote: Every part requires evaluating an algebraic expression at x = 5, directly matching substitute-into-expressions. No expansion or collection of like terms is required.
questions.methodNote: Example 19 substitutes the given value, evaluates brackets first, then multiplication and addition or subtraction. Examples 17–18 explain the implicit multiplication before brackets; page 16 reinforces substitution and operation order.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct substitution of one positive integer, followed by bracket evaluation and ordinary arithmetic.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct substitution of one positive integer, followed by bracket evaluation and arithmetic.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts assess substitution into bracketed algebraic expressions, directly matching Example 19. No expansion of brackets is required.
questions.methodNote: Example 19 substitutes the given value, evaluates brackets, multiplies, then performs remaining addition. Examples 17–18 establish multiplication by a bracketed expression; Example 21 reinforces substitution and operation order.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct substitution of one positive integer, followed by bracket evaluation and arithmetic.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute both values and coordinate products inside a bracket, subtraction, outer multiplication and final addition in the correct order.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts directly assess substitution into expressions. Part f combines two substituted products within brackets and a further product outside.
questions.methodNote: Substitute the given values, evaluate brackets, then multiply before adding. Example 19 demonstrates bracket substitution; Example 22 demonstrates substitution into a bracketed product.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct substitution of two positive whole-number values, followed by bracket evaluation and arithmetic.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate ordered operations while distinguishing a power of the variable from a power of the whole multiplied expression.

questions.mappingNote: Question 6 explicitly references Example 20. Parts a and d apply a power before multiplication; parts b and c apply a power to the product. Translating the operation order is the directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Example 20 distinguishes squaring a number before multiplication from squaring the complete product. Example 21 reinforces the corresponding distinction for squares and cubes. Write the coefficient before the pronumeral and use brackets when the power applies to the complete product.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate two successive operations into algebra, distinguishing a power of a pronumeral from a power of a complete product.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute x=4 and distinguish squaring x before multiplication from squaring the bracketed product.

questions.mappingNote: Question 7 directly parallels Example 21(a, b), replacing coefficient 2 with 5 and the substituted value 3 with 4. Substitution is the directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Example 21(a) expands the squared pronumeral as repeated multiplication before substitution. Example 21(b) substitutes within brackets and squares the entire product. Examples 19 and 20 establish substitution, operation order and the significance of brackets.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct substitution distinguishes squaring a pronumeral from squaring an entire product.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute x=2 and apply the cube to either x alone or the whole bracketed product, as indicated.

questions.mappingNote: Part a directly follows Example 21c, and part b follows Example 21d. Both assess substitution and evaluation while retaining the scope of the exponent.
questions.methodNote: Example 21c expands the variable's cube as repeated multiplication; Example 21d substitutes into the bracketed product before evaluating its cube. Examples 19–20 establish substitution and the distinction between powers with and without brackets.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct substitution into two cubic expressions, distinguishing a power of the variable from a power of the whole product.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute the given value, respect the different scopes of the square, and complete multiplication before the final addition.

questions.mappingNote: All three parts directly assess substitution; parts a and b square the bracketed product, while part c squares only the pronumeral before multiplying by 6.
questions.methodNote: Examples 19 and 21 substitute the given value, evaluate brackets and powers in the correct order, and then complete multiplication and addition. Example 20 distinguishes a squared product from a coefficient multiplying a square.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct substitution of one positive integer, distinguishing a squared product from a coefficient multiplying a square.

classification.difficultyReason: Express an increased quantity and then multiply it by the number of identical crates.

questions.mappingNote: Question 10 applies the same grouped-quantity method to crates: first n+2 per crate, then 5(n+2) altogether. It assesses translating words into expressions rather than expanding brackets.
questions.methodNote: Example 22 forms the quantity in each basket by addition, then multiplies the bracketed quantity by the number of baskets.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Express an increased quantity and then multiply it by the number of identical crates.

classification.difficultyReason: Separate seats per row from the number of rows, add four to each row's quantity, then multiply the whole updated quantity by 20.

questions.mappingNote: Question 11 transfers this method to rows of seats: x+4 seats per row multiplied by 20 rows. No numerical substitution or bracket expansion is requested.
questions.methodNote: Example 22 adds the extra items within each group before multiplying by the number of groups, retaining brackets around the group quantity.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify the increased number of seats per row and express the total across 20 rows without intermediate prompts.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct products of positive coefficients and simple pronumerals, using repeated factors to write powers.

questions.mappingNote: All eight parts directly assess multiplication of algebraic terms. Parts a–c multiply a number and a term; d–h combine coefficients and variable factors, including repeated variables.
questions.methodNote: Page 18 introduces the any-order property: collect numerical factors, group repeated pronumerals and write them as powers. Example 23a–c demonstrates these products and states that intermediate steps are not required.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct products of positive coefficients and simple pronumerals, using repeated factors to write powers.

classification.difficultyReason: Square a single algebraic term by multiplying its numerical and variable factors.

questions.mappingNote: Each part directly applies this method to the square of a numerical coefficient multiplied by one variable. Multiplying algebraic terms is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Example 23d and e expand a power into repeated factors, regroup numerical and variable factors, then simplify using powers.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Square a single algebraic term by multiplying its numerical and variable factors.

classification.difficultyReason: Simplify direct products of algebraic terms, including squared factors and repeated variables.

questions.mappingNote: Each part directly assesses multiplication of algebraic terms; parts a, b and e additionally require the source-taught treatment of a squared bracketed term.
questions.methodNote: Use the any-order property to multiply numerical factors and collect repeated letters into powers. Evaluate the power of a bracketed term first, as demonstrated in Example 23d–f.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Simplify direct products of algebraic terms, including squared factors and repeated variables.

classification.difficultyReason: Combines multiplication of several algebraic factors with powers of bracketed terms.

questions.mappingNote: Every part simplifies a product of algebraic terms; parts a, c, d and f also require squaring a bracketed term. This directly assesses multiplication of algebraic terms.
questions.methodNote: Use the any-order property to group numerical and letter factors. Expand powers of bracketed terms before multiplying, as demonstrated in Example 23, especially parts c–f.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combines multiplication of several algebraic factors with powers of bracketed terms.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the supplied rule directly, interpreting fourth and 100th as values of n before multiplying and adding.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts evaluate the supplied stick-count expression at a specified diagram position; deriving a new pattern rule is not required.
questions.methodNote: Page 9 defines substitution and demonstrates replacing a pronumeral before calculating. Page 20 Example 24 relates diagram position n to a dot-count expression. Pages 21–22 reinforce algebraic expressions and numerical substitution.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute two specified diagram numbers into the supplied linear expression.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate the labelled rectangle into a product, simplify x times x to a square, then evaluate the resulting area expression at given values.

questions.mappingNote: Part a applies Example 25 to sides 3x and 2x. Parts b and c apply the substitution method of Example 26 to the resulting area expression.
questions.methodNote: Use rectangle area as length multiplied by width, simplify the product of algebraic terms, then substitute and evaluate the power before multiplication. Page 21 Examples 25 and 26 demonstrate these steps; page 9 demonstrates substitution with powers.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Form an algebraic area expression from two variable side lengths, then evaluate it for two values.

classification.difficultyReason: Find two component areas using symbolic dimensions and add them.

questions.mappingNote: The supplied partition identifies a rectangle and a square, so the directly assessed task is composite area using algebraic products.
questions.methodNote: Page 21 Examples 25 and 26 calculate rectangle and square areas by multiplying side lengths. Example 27 adds the areas of two rectangles to obtain a total symbolic area.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find two component areas using symbolic dimensions and add them.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate the next whole number and next even number into expressions using the given term.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts require translating a verbal relationship into an expression based on 2n; no substitution or pattern table is required.
questions.methodNote: Page 4 translates verbal operations into algebraic expressions. Page 22, Example 28, uses the same given expression for the nth non-zero even number and applies the stated operation to it.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate the next whole number and next even number into expressions using the given term.

classification.difficultyReason: Match each component to the square or rectangle key, including rotated rectangles, then express the counted areas as multiples of m and n.

questions.mappingNote: Each given area is already known symbolically. The assessed step is counting repeated areas and collecting the m and n terms.
questions.methodNote: Example 27 adds the areas of separate rectangles and collects like terms. The area introduction identifies square and rectangle areas; page 12 explains collecting terms with matching pronumerals.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Count repeated square and rectangle areas and collect their contributions.

classification.difficultyReason: Determine whether algebraic expressions preserve divisibility by 5, distinguishing a factor of 5 from an offset.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed task is deciding divisibility by 5 from algebraic structure; numerical index evaluation and expansion are supporting skills rather than the primary task.
questions.methodNote: Use algebra to describe number patterns, interpreting products, sums and differences as in the expression table and Example 28. The question supplies the rule for generating further multiples of 5.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Determine whether algebraic expressions preserve divisibility by 5, distinguishing a factor of 5 from an offset.

classification.difficultyReason: Express adjacent even numbers, odd numbers and multiples using their constant differences.

questions.mappingNote: Each part translates a verbal relationship into an algebraic expression: add 2 for the next even number, add 3 and 6 for the next two multiples of 3, and subtract 2 for the previous odd number.
questions.methodNote: Page 22 introduces algebraic descriptions of number patterns through Example 28. Page 4 supports translating addition and subtraction descriptions into expressions. Use the constant difference between consecutive members of each sequence.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Express adjacent even numbers, odd numbers and multiples using their constant differences.

classification.difficultyReason: Determine parity from products and sums involving an even pronumeral.

questions.mappingNote: The question directly assesses divisibility by 2 in algebraic expressions; number-pattern expressions provide the supporting context.
questions.methodNote: Example 28 represents even numbers using a factor of 2 and interprets multiplication algebraically. Apply this representation and the parity of the added constant.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Determine parity from products and sums involving an even pronumeral.

classification.difficultyReason: Select the appropriate rectangle rule for each request, combining repeated sides for perimeter and multiplying algebraic lengths for area.

questions.mappingNote: Part a combines the rectangle perimeter rule with collecting like terms. Part b directly assesses multiplying algebraic terms in a rectangle-area context, so multiplication of algebraic terms is the primary skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 12 demonstrates collecting like terms. Page 20 gives rectangle area as the product of its side lengths; Example 25 on page 21 applies this to algebraic lengths. For perimeter, add the four side lengths and collect like terms.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply familiar rectangle formulas to algebraic side lengths and simplify sums and products.

classification.difficultyReason: Express a square's perimeter and area using its given pronumeral side length.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts apply algebraic notation to familiar square measurements; area explicitly assesses the convention for a repeated pronumeral factor.
questions.methodNote: Add the four equal side lengths and collect like terms for perimeter. For area, multiply the side length by itself and write the product as a square, following page 20 and Example 26 on page 21.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Express a square's perimeter and area using its given pronumeral side length.

classification.difficultyReason: Form perimeter and area expressions from a rectangle with a binomial side length, then simplify.

questions.mappingNote: The binomial side requires expansion when simplifying the area; perimeter also requires collecting like terms. The supplied reuse candidates assess different tasks and are not source-equivalent.
questions.methodNote: Add all four side lengths and collect like terms for perimeter. For area, multiply the rectangle's side lengths, then apply the distributive law. Pages 20–21 establish algebraic rectangle areas; page 12 demonstrates collecting like terms and the distributive law.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Form perimeter and area expressions from a rectangle with a binomial side length, then simplify.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate verbal operations into algebra, preserving subtraction and division order and using brackets when a whole sum is multiplied.

questions.mappingNote: Every part translates words into an algebraic expression. Parts c, g and h additionally use conventional product, power and fraction notation; part f requires parentheses around the sum.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 introduces pronumerals and translates addition and subtraction descriptions. Page 3 translates products, quotients and two-operation descriptions, retaining operation order.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate verbal operations into expressions, retaining subtraction order and grouping a sum before multiplication.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute the supplied values and follow operation order, particularly distinguishing a squared product from a coefficient multiplying a square.

questions.mappingNote: Each part directly evaluates an expression at the given values. Parts g and h distinguish squaring a product from multiplying a square.
questions.methodNote: Pages 9–10 define substitution and demonstrate replacing pronumerals, evaluating powers before multiplication, then adding or subtracting. Pages 6–7 explain implicit multiplication and powers; page 3 confirms the order of operations applies in algebra.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute two positive integers and evaluate sums, products and squares using the order of operations.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute the specified position into the supplied square-number formula and evaluate a square.

questions.mappingNote: The supplied nth-square formula requires substituting 12 for n, then evaluating the square; substitution is the primary assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 6 defines powers as repeated multiplication. Page 9 demonstrates substituting a particular value into a squared pronumeral and evaluating it.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute the specified position into the supplied square-number formula and evaluate a square.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute one positive integer into a supplied linear formula and evaluate.

questions.mappingNote: The supplied odd-number formula is evaluated at n=21; substitution is the directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 9 defines substitution and Example 11 replaces the pronumeral with its given value before evaluating multiplication and subtraction.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute one positive integer into a supplied linear formula and evaluate.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate a square's symbolic perimeter into an expression for one of its four equal sides.

questions.mappingNote: The task translates a perimeter description into an algebraic quotient; square perimeter knowledge supplies the divisor 4.
questions.methodNote: Use a pronumeral for an unknown number and express equal sharing by division, as in Example 7 on PDF page 4.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate a square's symbolic perimeter into an expression for one of its four equal sides.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate the total of three stated monetary amounts into an algebraic sum.

questions.mappingNote: The question directly assesses translating a verbal total into an algebraic expression; no numerical substitution or collection of like terms is required.
questions.methodNote: Use pronumerals for unknown quantities and addition for a total, following Example 2(e), which translates the sum of three quantities into an expression.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate the total of three stated monetary amounts into an algebraic sum.

classification.difficultyReason: Express an unknown addend by subtracting the known pronumeral from the given total.

questions.mappingNote: The total and one addend are given; the required expression translates the remaining-addend relationship into subtraction.
questions.methodNote: Represent an unknown number with a pronumeral and translate subtraction into an algebraic expression, following Examples 2 and 5.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Express an unknown addend by subtracting the known pronumeral from the given total.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine numerical factors and express repeated pronumeral factors using powers.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–c apply product and power notation; parts d–f additionally multiply numerical factors. Simplifying products of algebraic terms is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 6 introduces omitted multiplication signs, numerical coefficients first and repeated factors written as powers. Example 8 combines numerical factors and repeated pronumerals; page 7 consolidates these conventions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine numerical factors and express repeated pronumeral factors using powers.

classification.difficultyReason: Directly rewrite three division expressions using fraction notation.

questions.mappingNote: All three parts assess the same division-notation convention directly; no evaluation or algebraic simplification is required.
questions.methodNote: The notation-for-division section writes the dividend above the fraction bar and the divisor below it, explicitly demonstrating x divided by 5 as x/5.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Directly rewrite three division expressions using fraction notation.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate familiar product, quotient and power descriptions; simplify a product of terms and a cubed term.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–d assess translation and algebraic notation. Parts e–f additionally simplify products of algebraic terms; expanding the cube into three identical factors follows the taught repeated-factor method.
questions.methodNote: Translate operation words, write numerical coefficients first, represent division with a fraction, and express repeated variable factors using powers. Page 6 Example 8 multiplies numerical factors and combines repeated letters; page 7 identifies cubes and fourth powers.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate familiar product, quotient and power descriptions; simplify a product of terms and a cubed term.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute one positive integer into expressions, evaluating powers before multiplication and addition.

questions.mappingNote: All eight parts substitute x = 5 into a numerical expression; parts c, d, f, g and h also evaluate positive integer powers. Substitution is the directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Section 3C defines substitution. Examples 11–13 replace the pronumeral with its given value, then evaluate powers, multiplication and addition or subtraction in order.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute one positive integer into expressions, evaluating powers before multiplication and addition.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine coefficients of matching algebraic terms, retaining separate variable groups in part f.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–e combine coefficients of one matching term type, including xy and x squared. Part f collects x terms and y terms separately. These directly assess collect-like-terms.
questions.methodNote: Page 12 defines like terms by matching pronumerals and indices and explains adding their coefficients. Examples 15–16 on pages 12–13 collect matching terms and keep unlike terms separate.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine coefficients of matching algebraic terms, retaining separate variable groups in part f.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate two successive operations into an expression, using brackets to preserve their order.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts assess translating verbal operations into algebra with brackets; neither requires expanding the brackets.
questions.methodNote: Example 22 first forms the expression for the changed quantity, then uses brackets to multiply that entire expression by the number of groups.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate two successive operations into an expression, using brackets to preserve their order.

classification.difficultyReason: Expand squared and cubed products into repeated factors, then multiply coefficients and pronumerals.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts require multiplication of algebraic factors after interpreting powers of bracketed products. Multiplying and simplifying algebraic terms is the closest supplied skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 15, Example 20(b), expands a squared algebraic product into repeated factors before simplifying: (3a)^2 = 3a × 3a = 9a^2. Apply the same repeated-factor method to squares, cubes and subsequent multiplication.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Expand squared and cubed products into repeated factors, then multiply coefficients and pronumerals.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute one positive integer and evaluate expressions using brackets, multiplication and a square.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts directly assess substitution and numerical evaluation, rather than expansion or algebraic simplification.
questions.methodNote: Replace the pronumeral with its given value, then evaluate using the order of operations. Example 11 models single-variable substitution; Example 13 models evaluating a square before addition or subtraction.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute one positive integer and evaluate expressions using brackets, multiplication and a square.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate algebraic rectangle areas and subtract an inner area to find each frame's shaded area.

questions.mappingNote: Part a directly applies algebraic rectangle area. Parts b and c use the same area calculations, subtracting the unshaded inner region; composite area is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 20 gives rectangle area as the product of its side lengths and square area as x squared. Page 21 Examples 25–27 multiply algebraic side lengths and combine component areas.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate algebraic rectangle areas and subtract an inner area to find each frame's shaded area.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute into expressions containing brackets and distinguish squaring a product from multiplying a square.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts directly assess numerical substitution. Parts c and d require applying the exponent to the correct base.
questions.methodNote: Replace each pronumeral with its given value, then evaluate using brackets and powers before multiplication and subtraction. Examples 11–13 show substitution and successive aligned calculations, including powers.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute into expressions containing brackets and distinguish squaring a product from multiplying a square.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute a positive integer and evaluate using brackets, powers and division.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts directly assess substitution into expressions; powers, brackets and a fraction are arithmetic features of that method.
questions.methodNote: Replace the pronumeral with its given value, then evaluate in order, retaining substitution and intermediate arithmetic as in Examples 11–13.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute a positive integer and evaluate using brackets, powers and division.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute two given positive integers, respecting fraction grouping and evaluating powers before subtraction.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts directly assess substitution into expressions. Parts b and c distinguish division of an entire sum from division of a single term; part d requires evaluating both squares before subtracting.
questions.methodNote: Replace each pronumeral with its given value, then evaluate using the order of operations. Example 11 demonstrates fraction substitution; Example 12 demonstrates substitution with two pronumerals; Example 13 evaluates powers before other operations.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute two given positive integers, respecting fraction grouping and evaluating powers before subtraction.

classification.difficultyReason: Collect coefficients of like terms, including powers and products written in different variable orders.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts directly assess collecting like terms; part d additionally requires recognising that dc² and c²d are the same variable product.
questions.methodNote: Example 16 collects coefficients while retaining the variable factors and powers. Exercise 3D includes like terms with reversed variable order.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Collect coefficients of like terms, including powers and products written in different variable orders.

classification.difficultyReason: Express the square's area algebraically and identify the shaded fraction from its diagonal subdivisions.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed calculation is square area in terms of a, followed by equal-area subdivision. The rectangle-area skill includes squares; dissection is secondary.
questions.methodNote: Page 20 states that a square with side x cm has area x squared cm squared. Example 26 on page 21 derives a times a equals a squared. Apply this square-area method and the supplied diagonal subdivisions to identify one half or one quarter, without introducing an additional triangle-area formula.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Express the square's area algebraically and identify the shaded fraction from its diagonal subdivisions.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the supplied enclosing rectangles and subdivisions to recognise half-rectangle triangles, then combine two or four such areas algebraically.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed task is geometric decomposition into rectangle-related triangular regions, with algebraic multiplication and addition supporting the calculation.
questions.methodNote: Pages 20–21 teach rectangle area as the product of side lengths and combining algebraic areas; page 18 supports simplifying products and pages 12–13 support collecting like terms. Use the question's enclosing rectangles and subdivisions to derive the areas, rather than introducing a diagonal-area formula.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use enclosing rectangles and subdivisions to derive algebraic areas of triangles and a quadrilateral.

classification.difficultyReason: Carry an expression through the supplied sequence, distribute multiplication, collect terms and explain why cancellation returns the original number.

questions.mappingNote: The four dependent operations require translation, distribution in part b and collection of like terms in parts c–d. Expanding brackets is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 translates descriptions into expressions. Page 14 Example 17 places the preceding result in brackets before multiplying. Pages 12–13 explain distribution and collection of like terms. Pages 18, 20 and 21 provide multiplication and algebraic-expression context.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate successive operations into algebra, expand a bracket and explain why the result is the original number.

classification.difficultyReason: Deduce a binomial identity by equating the area of a partitioned rectangle with the sum of its four regions, then calculate algebraic perimeters.

questions.mappingNote: The most advanced directly assessed task is deducing a binomial product identity from four rectangular areas. Use the supplied subdivision before collecting like terms; do not replace the requested deduction by an unexplained expansion formula.
questions.methodNote: Pages 20–21 teach rectangle area as the product of its side lengths and total area as the sum of component areas. Pages 12–13 teach collecting like terms; page 18 teaches products such as x times x = x squared. Pages 3 and 14 support translating side-length sums and bracketed products. The partitioned rectangle in this question supplies the local area model for the deduction.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Deduce a binomial identity by equating the area of a partitioned rectangle with the sum of its four regions, then calculate algebraic perimeters.

classification.difficultyReason: Infer missing boundary lengths, combine algebraic perimeter terms and split an L-shaped region into rectangles.

questions.mappingNote: Composite area is the most advanced directly assessed geometric skill. Perimeter, missing rectilinear sides and collecting like terms support the two responses.
questions.methodNote: Page 6 demonstrates coefficient multiplication and algebraic notation. Pages 20–21 teach rectangle area as the product of side lengths and addition of algebraic rectangle areas. Apply those methods after dissecting the L-shape; find perimeter by adding its boundary lengths.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Infer missing boundary lengths, combine algebraic perimeter terms and split an L-shaped region into rectangles.

classification.difficultyReason: Investigate possible final digits, then justify a divisibility statement for every even whole number.

questions.mappingNote: Divisibility is the most advanced directly assessed skill, particularly in parts c–d. Substitution and evaluation of squares support parts a–b. The supplied examples remain visible question givens.
questions.methodNote: Page 6 defines powers as repeated multiplication. Pages 9–10 demonstrate substituting numerical values and evaluating powers before addition. Apply these methods to the possible final digits; part d requires a general remainder argument rather than finite examples alone.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Investigate possible final digits, then justify a divisibility statement for every even whole number.

classification.difficultyReason: Complete a numerical table, identify an invariant difference and justify the identity for every whole number using distribution and cancellation.

questions.mappingNote: The most advanced directly assessed task is proving the binomial product identity in part c; table substitution and collecting like terms are supporting skills. The identity is a requested challenge deduction, rather than a previously supplied teaching rule.
questions.methodNote: Use algebraic multiplication and power notation, substitute numerical values in expressions, and compare the resulting table columns. For the requested general explanation, distribute each term and collect the cancelling like terms, as independently confirmed by the teacher solution. Do not assume a memorised special-product formula.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Complete a numerical table, identify an invariant difference and justify the identity for every whole number using distribution and cancellation.

bankProjection.note: Source-confirmed category headings are omitted only from bank prompts and presentation. Explicit equivalent fraction notation repairs satisfy bank validation. Source booklet content and all questions are retained.
